questions.prompt: What is a key difference between a message queue and an event log (like Kafka)?

options.text: A queue keeps messages forever; a log deletes them immediately
A queue removes a message once consumed; a log retains ordered messages that consumers read by offset and can replay
A log can only have one consumer

questions.explanation: A queue removes each message on consume (workers compete); a log retains ordered messages so many consumers read independently by offset and can replay history.

questions.prompt: What is the main downside of at-least-once delivery?

options.text: The same message may be delivered more than once (duplicates)
It cannot be used with queues

questions.explanation: At-least-once never loses messages, but a lost acknowledgment can cause redelivery, so consumers may see duplicates and must handle them idempotently.

questions.prompt: Why is true exactly-once DELIVERY generally impossible in a distributed system?

options.text: Because a sender with no acknowledgment can't tell if the message or the ack was lost, so it must risk loss or duplication

questions.explanation: The ambiguity of a missing acknowledgment forces a choice between at-most-once (risk loss) and at-least-once (risk duplicates). Exactly-once delivery can't be guaranteed.

questions.prompt: How do real systems achieve 'exactly-once processing'?

options.text: By combining at-least-once delivery with idempotent (or deduplicating) consumers

questions.explanation: At-least-once delivery plus an idempotent consumer (or dedup by message id) means processing a duplicate has no extra effect — 'effectively once.'

questions.prompt: Does Kafka's 'exactly-once semantics' guarantee exactly-once end-to-end to an external database or email service?

options.text: No — it holds within Kafka; writing to an external system still needs an idempotent sink
No, Kafka has no exactly-once features at all

questions.explanation: Kafka's exactly-once (idempotent producer + transactions) applies within Kafka. End-to-end exactly-once to an external sink still requires that sink to be idempotent.

questions.prompt: Coping when producers push faster than consumers can handle is called ______. (one word)
questions.explanation: Backpressure covers buffering, scaling consumers, or slowing/rejecting producers. Unbounded queues hide overload, so monitor consumer lag and cap growth.
